title: Crypto tax litigation
excerpt: Taxpayer defence against information requests, limited reviews, audits and penalties issued by the Spanish tax authority (AEAT) in relation to crypto assets. We respond within the deadline and build the documentary and on-chain evidence that supports your position.

hero.subheading: If you have a notice from the AEAT on your desk, the deadline comes first. We respond to information requests, file submissions and appeals, and build the documentary and on-chain evidence behind every figure.

sections.body:
Receiving a notice from the Spanish tax authority about your crypto assets does not mean you have done something wrong. It means the AEAT holds a figure that does not match your tax return, and that it is now up to you to explain where each number comes from. The difference between a procedure that closes quietly and one that ends in an assessment and a penalty almost always comes down to two things: responding within the deadline, and being able to evidence the origin of every transaction.

Since DAC8 came into force and automatic information exchange between exchanges and tax administrations began, the AEAT no longer depends on you declaring: it cross-checks what platforms report against what appears in your income tax return. When those two figures diverge, a procedure opens. And with crypto assets there are many legitimate reasons why they might diverge: internal transfers between your own wallets counted as disposals, swaps left undeclared through simple unawareness, automated reports with reconciliation errors, or defunct exchanges whose history you can no longer download.

Our ground here is compliance and the defence of your tax position. We do not promise a specific outcome or anticipate how a resolution will go: we work on what can actually be built, which is a documented, traceable and defensible position.

bullets: Responses to information requests: we assess the real scope of what is being asked, reconstruct the activity for the tax year in question and prepare the response with its supporting documentation, within the deadline granted.

Limited reviews and verification procedures: assistance throughout the procedure, control over the limits of what the administration may examine in each type of action, and responses to successive requests.
Tax audits: representation and assistance before the inspector, preparation of documentation ahead of each appearance, and case management through to the final report.

Submissions and appeals: submissions against the proposed assessment, administrative appeal (recurso de reposición) and economic-administrative claim before the TEAR or TEAC depending on amount and subject matter.

Appeals against penalties: analysis of the subjective element of the infringement, which in crypto assets is usually where the defence lies: a reasonable interpretation of the rules and the absence of concealment.

Documentary and on-chain evidence: reconstruction of the transaction history, identification of internal transfers, wallet-to-wallet traceability and preparation of the expert report accompanying the submissions.
Voluntary regularisation: where no procedure has yet opened, analysis of the supplementary return route and its consequences before the administration moves first.

steps.title: Reading the notice and calculating the deadline
steps.body: The first step is knowing exactly which procedure has opened, which tax years it covers and how many working days remain. An information request, a limited review and an audit have very different scopes and consequences, and the clock starts from notification, not from when you read it.

steps.title: Reconstructing the year's activity
steps.body: We consolidate your data from exchanges, wallets and protocols until we have the complete history for the period requested. This is usually where the source of the discrepancy appears: transfers between your own wallets recorded as disposals, undeclared swaps, or staking rewards never attributed.

steps.title: Comparison against what was filed
steps.body: We compare the actual activity against your filed return and against the figure the AEAT is working from. We quantify the difference, identify its cause, and determine which part is a genuine error and which is a matter of interpretation or of incomplete data on the administration's side.

steps.title: Strategy and written response
steps.body: We define the position to argue and prepare the submission with its supporting evidence. We explain beforehand what will be argued, what backs each point, and which scenarios may follow, including the unfavourable ones.

steps.title: Filing and case follow-up
steps.body: We file within the deadline and follow the case through to resolution, responding to any successive requests and keeping you informed of every development.

steps.title: Appeal, where appropriate
steps.body: If the resolution is unfavourable, we assess with you whether appealing is worthwhile given the amount, the grounds and the cost of the procedure, and we prepare the administrative appeal or economic-administrative claim.

bullets: Data and judgement in one place: most crypto tax procedures are not won on legal argument but by evidencing where each euro comes from. We reconstruct the activity ourselves, without relying on a third-party automated report.

We review transaction by transaction: a software-generated report is a starting point, never the deliverable. In an open procedure, a poor reconciliation is exactly what the administration will challenge.
On-chain traceability: we know how to reconstruct a wallet's trail when the exchange no longer exists or the downloadable history is incomplete, one of the most frequent problems in these cases.
Explicit deadlines: from day one we tell you how many working days remain, what we need from you, and the date by which the response must be closed.
Chartered tax advice: the case is handled by a chartered tax adviser, with the professional liability that entails.
No scaremongering: penalties are explained when relevant and with their legal basis, never as a sales argument.

items.title: Information request over differences between exchange reporting and the tax return
items.body: The most common scenario. The AEAT receives the traded volume from the exchange and finds no matching figure in the return. In many cases the difference is not hidden gain but internal transfers between the taxpayer's own wallets that the report counts as transactions. The defence consists of reconstructing the full history and evidencing ownership of the destination addresses.

items.title: Undeclared prior years surfacing when the current one is filed
items.body: A taxpayer correctly files the current year and in doing so makes visible undeclared activity from earlier years. The route here is usually voluntary regularisation through a supplementary return before a procedure opens, weighing the effect of surcharges against that of an assessment with a penalty.

items.title: Automated report with reconciliation errors already filed with the administration
items.body: The taxpayer answered an initial request with a software-generated report containing duplicates, mispriced swaps or zero acquisition cost on received tokens. The administration takes it as the taxpayer's own declaration. Redoing the reconciliation and documenting the discrepancy with what was already filed is a different and more delicate job than doing it properly from the start.

items.title: Penalty where a reasonable interpretation of the rules exists
items.body: Assessment accepted but penalty appealed. In crypto assets, much of the activity — swaps, staking, airdrops, DeFi — went years without clear administrative criteria. The absence of concealment and the existence of a reasonable interpretation are the core of an appeal against the penalty element.

items.title: Audit requesting the history of a defunct exchange
items.body: Documentation is requested from a platform that has shut down and whose history can no longer be downloaded. The reconstruction relies on on-chain traceability, bank statements for fiat in and out, and coherent circumstantial evidence across sources.

items.q: How long do I have to answer an information request?
items.a: The usual deadline for answering an information request is ten working days from notification, though it varies with the type of procedure and what the notice itself states. The clock runs from the date of notification, not from when the document is opened, and for electronic notifications it is deemed served ten calendar days after being made available if not accessed sooner. The first thing we do on receiving a case is calculate the real deadline.

items.q: What is the difference between an information request, a limited review and an audit?
items.a: An information request asks for specific data and does not necessarily mean you are being reviewed. A limited review is a management procedure with a restricted scope: the administration may examine certain elements but cannot inspect commercial accounting records. An audit has the widest scope and is conducted by an inspector. Each carries different consequences and deadlines, and responding to one as though it were another is a common mistake.

items.q: How many tax years back can the AEAT review?
items.a: The administration's right to assess lapses four years after the end of the filing deadline, a period interrupted by any notified action. There are situations in which that calculation changes, so the specific limitation position in your case must be analysed against the actual dates in the file.

items.q: Can I respond myself and call you only if it gets complicated?
items.a: You can, but bear in mind that whatever you submit in the first response stays in the file and shapes everything that follows. Correcting a report already submitted is harder than getting it right the first time. If you are going to respond on your own, at least check that the figures you provide are reconstructable and consistent with what you filed.

items.q: What if I no longer have the complete history of my transactions?
items.a: This is common, particularly with platforms that have closed. The reconstruction relies on what does exist: on-chain traceability of the wallets, bank statements for fiat in and out, confirmation emails and partial third-party data. It does not always reach one hundred per cent, but it does reach a documented and coherent position.

items.q: Do you work with other firms?
items.a: Yes. We provide technical support to accountants and law firms without crypto specialisation who are handling the procedure and need the activity reconstructed along with the expert report that supports it.

items.q: Can you guarantee there will be no penalty?
items.a: No. Nobody can anticipate how a resolution will go, and you should be wary of anyone who claims otherwise. What we can do is build the best documented position possible with the available data, explain the possible scenarios frankly — including the unfavourable ones — and respond within the deadline, which is where many cases are lost.
